title: Power Transition and the Rise of China

cards.h: The defining rivalry of the century
cards.b:
The rise of China and the US response shape trade, technology, security and India's choices. Theory frames it: power transition, Thucydides Trap and offensive realism. UPSC links this to the changing world order and India's China policy.

Expect this as a 10 or 15 mark question, or as a supporting example inside a longer answer. Read the cards in order, then test yourself with the quiz.
A.F.K. Organski, World Politics (1958), and Kugler. Unlike balance of power, it says war is likeliest near parity, not when one side dominates.

Graham Allison, Destined for War (2017), took Thucydides' line that Sparta's fear of rising Athens made war inevitable. In 16 historical cases of a rising power challenging a ruling one, 12 ended in war. Allison says war between the US and China is not inevitable but is more likely than we think. Critics say the sample is selective and nuclear weapons change the logic.

John Mearsheimer, The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001): great powers seek regional hegemony, so a strong China will try to dominate Asia and the US will resist. G. John Ikenberry answers that the US-led liberal order is open and rules-based, so China can be integrated, though it is now strained. Joseph Nye's 'smart power' and the soft power view stress attraction.

• Reform from 1978 (Deng); WTO entry in 2001; world's second-largest economy since about 2010.
  • State capitalism, manufacturing, exports; Made in China 2025 push for technology.
  • Belt and Road (2013), AIIB (2016), BRICS and NDB, Global Development, Security and Civilisation initiatives.
  • PLA modernisation: carriers, missiles, South China Sea bases.

Obama's pivot to Asia (2011), the 2018 trade war under Trump, export controls on chips, and tariffs. Alliances: Quad (revived 2017), AUKUS (2021), Indo-Pacific strategy. As of 2025, tariff and technology rivalry continues alongside periodic truces, so describe the competition as managed rivalry and 'decoupling' and 'de-risking'.

• China's official line: 'peaceful development', a 'community with a shared future'.
  • Neighbours see assertiveness: South China Sea, Senkaku, Taiwan, the Himalayan border.
  • Domestic limits: ageing population, property debt, slower growth ('peak China').
  • Some scholars argue power transition applies poorly: the US is still ahead in alliances and technology, so a multipolar world or a G2 may emerge instead.

China wants a bigger say in institutions (IMF quota, UNSC, WTO) and builds alternatives, such as the AIIB and SCO. It does not directly attack the UN system, which it uses. Compare with the Soviet challenge: no ideological export, but a rival model of development (the 'Beijing Consensus').

India has the 1962 war, Doklam (2017), Galwan (June 2020), trade deficit, CPEC through PoK, 'string of pearls' in the Indian Ocean. India uses multi-alignment: Quad, I2U2, Russia ties, BRICS and SCO. Since the October 2024 patrolling arrangement and the Modi-Xi meetings (Kazan 2024; Tianjin SCO 2025), there has been a careful thaw, though trust is low.

"Does the power transition theory explain the US-China rivalry?"
"Examine the Thucydides Trap and its critics."
"Assess the implications of China's rise for India."

Structure: theory, Allison, Mearsheimer vs Ikenberry, China's tools, US response, debate, India.

Marks tip: open with a one-line definition, use two or three named thinkers, cases or Articles, add one Indian example, and end with a balanced, forward-looking line. Keep within the word limit.
